title: The world as dream
hookLine: a dream, a show, a bubble on water: the ninth Guru's pictures of a passing world

lines: THE HALF SECOND AFTER A DREAM.
cards: There's a half second, just after a vivid dream, when the dream is still the real world. The argument is still going. The house is still that strange house.
Then the ceiling comes into focus, a car passes outside, and the whole thing drains away like water from a sink. Nothing in it was lost, because none of it was ever held.
Near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Tegh Bahadur keeps coming back to that half second. Again and again, his saloks hold up the world and say: look, a dream.

teach.h: A DREAM, A SHOW, A BUBBLE.
teach.b: Two of his saloks, paraphrased. The first: know this world as a dream and a passing show; in it, Nanak, nothing is true except the Lord.

The second: as a bubble rises on water and bursts, again and again, so the world is made; listen, friend, says Nanak. A dream, a show, a bubble: real enough to see, too quick to keep. Here's what the dream does not mean.

It doesn't mean nothing matters. The same Guru stayed a householder, traveled to visit his Sikhs, and stood up for other people's faith with his life. You don't do that for a world you think is worthless.
One way Sikhs read these saloks: the dream is real as a dream. People, work, love, all of it is worth doing. What's untrue is the idea that any of it will stay.
The mistake isn't living in the dream; it's clutching at it, as if the bubble could go in a pocket. And the cure isn't to tear the world down.
It's to wake up: to notice, while you're still inside it, that the One who is true was there all along.
A slammed alarm clock wakes you angry.

A curtain opened slowly wakes you well. The saloks open the curtain one line at a time. And if life ever feels like it doesn't matter at all, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, or reach local emergency help.

how: Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks, with their images of the world as a dream and a bubble, are read near the close of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, including the readings families hold after a death.

games.q: what does “the world as dream” mean?
o: a world that passes like a dream; only the Lord is true
a habit of writing down your dreams each morning
the belief that nothing in life matters at all

games.q: the saloks' pictures: tap the pairs.
p: rises and bursts, again and again
the one thing the salok calls true

s: the saloks mean nothing in the world matters
the same Guru stayed a householder and gave his life for others; the dream is real while it lasts, it just doesn't stay.
one salok compares the world to a bubble on water
it rises and bursts, again and again.
the cure the saloks point to is tearing the world down
they point to waking: noticing the One who is true, while still inside the dream.

games.q: you've just heard the ninth Guru's salok: know this world as a dream. what do you do with your day?
o: give up on it: none of it is real.
grip it harder before it disappears.
live it fully, holding it lightly, remembering the One.
games.why: the Guru stayed a householder and served to the end. the saloks warn against clutching, not against living.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you've been gripping hard, a plan, a worry, a grudge, a thing you want badly, and don't throw it away.

Look at it the way you'd look at a dream you're slowly waking from, real while it lasts, not forever, and with each breath out let the room come into focus around it. If you pray, rest in Waheguru, the one the saloks call true.

wordCard.voice: The world as dream. In the ninth Guru's saloks, the world is a dream, a show, a bubble on water, and nothing in it stays except the Lord. Today's word.

orig.note: a dream; the ninth Guru's saloks ask us to know the world as a dream and a passing show.

carryVoice: Your line: wake up gently. A curtain opened slowly, never a slammed alarm. Rest well.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Salok Mahala 9, Ang 1427 (jio supna ar pekhna: the world as a dream and a show)
